verdict.why_winner: A targets a real, high-frequency, high-stakes pain: chasing statutory lien waivers is a notorious construction AP headache, and a non-statutory waiver in CA can leave a customer exposed to liens. It also fills a precise gap next to a feature Ramp ships today. The steps are concrete and demoable in 10 days: generate the statutory form, e-sign, chase, diff the returned scan word-for-word, and trigger the unconditional waiver once payment clears. The work is technically meaty, with document AI, deterministic statutory diffing and payment-event orchestration, and the result looks like something Ramp could actually ship.

ideas.label: A
ideas.concern: The 'dollars with a clock on them' framing is clever, but this is Ideas B and D stapled together. Voice-call-to-merchant also risks looking like theater if it's a teammate answering the phone.

ideas.label: C
ideas.concern: Ramp for Construction already validates waivers, and Siteline/Procore Pay already generate, send and chase them, so the delta is 'chase from inside Ramp' plus a word-level diff against statutory text. Judges will spend the first 90 seconds learning what a conditional waiver is, and the team has no realistic way to show the unconditional-waiver-after-payment step without the sandbox clearing a payment.

ideas.label: D
ideas.concern: Real gap: Ramp tells you to book stale checks to a liability and reissue manually, and nobody at Ramp owns escheatment. The vendor outreach, ACH-detail collection with fraud verification, and reissue loop are demoable in the sandbox, and the NAUPA export is a concrete artifact. But half the pitch (3-5 year dormancy tracking, due-diligence letters) runs entirely on synthetic data, the trigger is annual, and the fraud check on new ACH details is exactly where a student team will hand-wave.

verdict.why_winner: B is the project most likely to be fully working on demo day: one workflow, a real test harness (Stripe Issuing disputes), a clear agent loop from detection to evidence to merchant contact to a reason-coded packet with a countdown, and a one-click approval gate that shows product judgment. It doesn't duplicate what Ramp ships (we flag, we don't dispute for you), and the live merchant call is the kind of moment that wins a 4-minute demo. D is close and more original, but too much of it has to be simulated; A is B plus D with the same headcount.

The live voice call is a great demo moment but fragile; team must have a recorded fallback. Dollar impact per customer is modest, which caps the 'why does this matter' argument.

ideas.label: B
ideas.concern: Ramp already validates waivers and Siteline/Procore Pay already chase them, so this reads as a feature gap filler rather than automating an outdated workflow. Word-for-word statutory diffing of scanned waivers is genuinely hard OCR work that will likely look brittle in 10 days, and a generalist judging panel will spend a third of the 3-5 minutes on a construction-finance primer.

ideas.label: C
ideas.concern: Ramp genuinely has no escheatment feature and the stale-check reissue loop is real, but the headline part (dormancy tracking, due-diligence letters, NAUPA reports) is an annual compliance job that can only be shown on fabricated multi-year data, so judges can't tell if it works. Vendor ACH re-collection by phone/email is also the single highest-fraud-risk workflow in AP; a student team's 'verify against fraud' step will likely be hand-waved.

ideas.label: D
ideas.concern: The 'every dollar with a clock on it' framing is the best story in the set and the deadline board is a strong demo surface, but it is literally Idea A plus Idea C: two detection models, two outreach scripts, two action paths (Visa dispute packet vs ACH reissue with fraud checks). A 2-3 person team in 10 days will ship one path well and one as slides; I'd rather see A done deeply than D done halfway.

verdict.why_winner: A is the most credibly demoable project in 10 days: Stripe Issuing test-mode gives real dispute objects, the inbox-evidence and reason-code packet are concrete AI work Ramp does not ship today, and the flow from flagged charge to merchant email/call to one-click admin approval is a tight 4-minute story a generalist judge can follow without a primer. It fits the prompt (manual dispute form is the outdated workflow), avoids duplicating Ramp beyond the detection step, and its scope is small enough that the technical execution score (35% of rubric) can actually be earned. D tells a better story but is A plus C in the same timeline; B is the loser because Ramp and two competitors already cover most of it and the statutory-diff OCR is the part most likely to break on stage.

ideas.label: A
ideas.concern: Ramp already validates attached waivers, and Siteline and Procore Pay already chase them. The team must show the full collect, chase, statutory-diff and unconditional-on-clear loop actually closing a gap, then explain lien waivers fast to non-construction judges.

ideas.label: B
ideas.concern: It stitches two unrelated workflows (card disputes and stale-check reissue) into one pitch. In 10 days that likely means two half-built pipelines plus a fragile voice-call component, and a cluttered 4-minute demo with no single sharp story.

ideas.label: C
ideas.concern: Disputes are infrequent and low-dollar for most Ramp customers, and Ramp already flags duplicates. The voice-call merchant negotiation risks being a gimmick that fails live, leaving a well-built tool for a modest pain.

ideas.label: D
ideas.concern: Few Ramp customers pay vendors by paper check, and escheatment plays out over years. The dormancy and NAUPA portion runs entirely on synthetic data, so the demo shows a report generator for a problem judges will doubt is urgent.

verdict.why_winner: A targets a concrete, documented gap Ramp itself leaves open: collecting waivers, chasing vendors, and triggering the unconditional waiver after payment clears. The payoff is tangible, since an unwaived lien is real money and legal risk. It also has a technically interesting, verifiable core: generating the statutory form and diffing returned scans word-for-word against it. That chains cleanly into a crisp end-to-end demo (generate → e-sign → chase → diff catches a non-statutory edit → Ramp payment clears → unconditional requested) that a 2-3 person team can actually finish in 10 days.

ideas.label: A
ideas.concern: Genuine gap and a truly outdated workflow, but the escheatment half runs on synthetic multi-year data and the pain is annual and low-frequency; the demo risks feeling like a compliance report generator rather than a live agent.

ideas.label: B
ideas.concern: Two end-to-end workflows (Visa disputes plus check reissue/escheatment) with voice calls in 10 days almost certainly yields two half-finished flows; the 'deadline board' framing is nice but won't rescue broken plumbing on demo day.

ideas.label: C
ideas.concern: Ramp for Construction already validates waivers and Siteline/Procore Pay already chase them, so the differentiated slice is thin; judges will need a construction law primer, eating demo time and clarity.

ideas.label: D
ideas.concern: Dollar impact per company is modest and Ramp already surfaces duplicates, so the team must show the dispute-filing and merchant-call automation carries the weight; a flaky live voice call would sink the demo.

verdict.why_winner: D is the tightest scope that can plausibly ship working, end-to-end code in 10 days: Stripe Issuing test-mode gives a credible dispute pipeline, inbox evidence gathering plus a live merchant call shows off current AI tooling, and the one-click approval packet lands squarely on a gap Ramp's help center admits is manual. A is more creative but harder to demo without synthetic data, B tries to do both and will likely spread thin, and C duplicates what Ramp and competitors already ship.

ideas.label: A
ideas.concern: Ramp for Construction already validates waivers, so the team must show the delta (statutory generation, e-sign collection, word-for-word diff, conditional-to-unconditional handoff on payment clear) within the first 60 seconds, or judges will see a duplicate. Non-construction judges also need a tight primer.

ideas.label: B
ideas.concern: Disputes are infrequent and low-dollar per company. The live voice call to a merchant is flashy but fragile on stage, and Stripe test-mode disputes may feel staged rather than proving real recovery value.

ideas.label: C
ideas.concern: Bundling two unrelated workflows (Visa disputes and stale-check reissue) into one 'clock' narrative will likely produce two half-built pipelines in 10 days. The unifying deadline board is a thin wrapper rather than real shared logic.

ideas.label: D
ideas.concern: The pain is annual and niche, and the core escheatment value plays out over multi-year dormancy that must run on synthetic data. The demo boils down to reissuing a check by ACH plus a generated report, which is hard to make compelling in 3-5 minutes.

verdict.why_winner: A targets a real, high-stakes gap: CA voids non-statutory waivers, and unpaid subs can lien the property. It extends rather than duplicates Ramp's existing check by closing the loop: generating, sending, chasing and diffing waivers, then triggering the unconditional waiver off Ramp's payment event. The statutory text diff is a concrete, verifiable technical demo, and the scope fits a single coherent workflow in 10 days.

ideas.label: A
ideas.concern: Ramp already flags duplicates and the manual dispute form takes a couple of minutes; the pain being automated is modest and infrequent, so the project risks being a flashy voice-call demo wrapped around a thin workflow. Stripe Issuing test-mode disputes make it credible, but I'd want to see the evidence-gathering and reason-code logic actually work on messy inbox data rather than canned emails.

ideas.label: B
ideas.concern: The differentiated piece (collection, chasing, statutory text diff) sits on top of validation Ramp already ships and competes with Siteline and Procore Pay, so the novel surface area is small. Judges will need a primer on conditional vs unconditional waivers before the demo makes sense, and e-signature chasing is hard to show convincingly in 3-5 minutes. Highest risk of 'Ramp already does this' in the room.

ideas.label: C
ideas.concern: Two end-to-end agents (card disputes plus stale-check reissue), each with inbox mining, outbound voice, and a filing step, is too much for a 2-3 person team in 10 days. The likely outcome is two half-working paths and a demo that has to hand-wave one of them. The 'deadline board' framing is strong, but the team should pick one leak and ship it.

ideas.label: D
ideas.concern: Escheatment is annual and niche, and the multi-year dormancy tracking and NAUPA reporting can only be shown on synthetic data, which weakens the demo's credibility. The team must make the vendor-contact and ACH-verification step genuinely fraud-aware (callback verification, domain checks), otherwise the agent becomes a vendor-impersonation vector, which Ramp cares about a lot.

verdict.why_winner: D attacks a gap Ramp genuinely does not cover: voided checks today are dumped into a liability account and forgotten, and unclaimed-property compliance is a real, painful, and poorly tooled finance workflow. The near-term half (watch Bill Pay for voided checks, reach the vendor, verify ACH details, reissue through Ramp) is fully demoable in the sandbox and technically substantive, while the escheatment letters and NAUPA output add a creative, defensible long tail even if shown on synthetic data. A is a cleaner demo but automates a two-minute form on top of detection Ramp already does; C has the best framing but will spread the team too thin; B duplicates Ramp and two incumbents and needs a construction primer to land with judges.

ideas.label: A
ideas.concern: This is C and D stapled together under a 'deadline board' framing. In 10 days, both halves likely ship shallow: the dispute flow, voice call, evidence gathering, ACH reissue and escheatment logic are each a real project. The unifying story doesn't make either workflow better, and a 3-5 minute demo of two flows will feel rushed.

ideas.label: B
ideas.concern: The pain is real, and the word-for-word statutory diff is a concrete technical hook. But Ramp already validates waivers, and Siteline and Procore Pay already collect and chase them, so the gap is narrow: sending documents for e-signature and following up. Most judges will need a construction primer that eats into demo time.

ideas.label: C
ideas.concern: Disputes are infrequent and dollar amounts are modest, so the ROI story is thin unless they frame recovered dollars across a portfolio. The live voice call to a merchant could be gimmicky or flaky in a live demo, so they need a recorded fallback.

ideas.label: D
ideas.concern: This happens rarely, and the key multi-year dormancy logic runs on synthetic data, so the demo is mostly generating reports. Having an agent phone vendors to collect new ACH details is a classic payment-fraud vector, which a Ramp judge will immediately poke at. The NAUPA formatting for 3 states is compliance busywork rather than an AI showcase.

verdict.why_winner: C is a single focused workflow with a clear gap in Ramp: duplicates are flagged, but the dispute is a manual form against a hard 60-day window. It can be demoed end-to-end on real rails with Stripe Issuing test-mode disputes. The flow from detection to inbox evidence to merchant outreach to a reason-coded packet to one-click approval is meaty enough for strong technical execution and makes a crisp, legible 4-minute demo. A tries to do this plus D and will be thinner, B fights existing Ramp and competitor features, and D is niche with synthetic data and fraud risk.

ideas.label: A
ideas.concern: Genuinely white space for Ramp and a real compliance headache, but the escheatment half (dormancy tracking, due-diligence letters, NAUPA files for 3 states) is annual, runs entirely on synthetic multi-year data, and the ACH fraud-verification step is hand-wavy; in 10 days the credible demo is only the vendor-contact-and-reissue loop, and a judge will ask why the state-reporting piece isn't just a template.

ideas.label: B
ideas.concern: The 'every dollar with a clock on it' framing is the best narrative of the four, but two detection pipelines, two outreach flows, two filing paths and two sandboxes in 10 days almost guarantees both halves are shallow; most likely outcome is a nice deadline dashboard with one working path and one mocked path, which the rubric's 35% technical weight will punish.

ideas.label: C
ideas.concern: Ramp already surfaces duplicates and already has an in-app dispute initiation, so the team must show the agent is clearly additive (inbox evidence, cancellation-email proof, merchant call, reason-code packet) rather than a wrapper on a form; disputes are also infrequent and small per company, so the dollar impact story is weaker than the pitch implies.

ideas.label: D
ideas.concern: Ramp for Construction already validates waivers and Siteline/Procore Pay already collect and chase them, so the differentiated piece shrinks to statutory-text diffing and the conditional-to-unconditional handoff; a non-construction judging panel will spend half the demo on a primer, and the e-signature chase loop is table-stakes automation rather than a new AI capability.

verdict.why_winner: C is the most focused, most buildable idea with the most credible end-to-end demo: Stripe Issuing test-mode disputes give real inputs, the inbox-evidence-plus-live-voice-call loop is visually compelling in 3-5 minutes, and the Visa reason-code packet with one-click approval is a concrete, finishable artifact. It scores highest on the two heaviest rubric lines (technical execution and demo clarity) without the synthetic-data gap of A, the scope risk of B, or the overlap with existing products in D. D loses because it duplicates both Ramp's own waiver validation and dedicated competitors, leaving too little novel surface to justify the construction primer the audience would need.
